scope.start: 7a: Rav Acha of Difti asks which doubtful animals are tithed, continuing the *ma'aser behemah* proof from 6b
scope.end: 8a: 'they divide' means dividing the value, proved from two people sitting on an animal

sections.title: Tithing 'Doubtful' Animals: A Doubtful *Bekhor* or Its Redemption Lamb?
sections.gist: Continuing the proof that the court takes a seized doubtful animal back from the kohen: the tithed 'doubtful' animals can't be doubtful firstborns, which are already sacred, so they must be lambs that redeemed doubtful firstborn donkeys.

bullets.text: Background: the previous daf concluded that when the burden of proof falls on the claimant, the court is ruling that the holder owns the item, not just declining to act. So a kohen who grabs the animal must give it back, even though in matters of *issur* the doubt may remain.
Rav Acha of Difti asks Ravina: which doubtful animals does the Mishnah say enter the pen for *ma'aser behemah*?

Not a doubtful firstborn (*bekhor*). "The tenth shall be sacred" means the tithe becomes sacred through the tithing, which excludes an animal that is already sacred. A doubtful firstborn already carries that sanctity.
Rather, the case is a lamb given to redeem a donkey whose firstborn status is doubtful (*pidyon peter chamor*).

Rav Nachman in the name of Rabba bar Avuh: an Israelite with ten doubtful firstborn donkeys separates ten lambs to redeem them and tithes the lambs. All of them stay his, since the kohen can't prove a claim to any one of them.

Even if the donkey really was a firstborn, the redemption lamb has no sanctity of its own; at most it is money owed to the kohen. So the only question is who owns it. Because the Israelite is ruled the owner, not merely left holding it, the lamb can count toward his tithe.

sections.title: The Bathhouse: Consecrating What You Can't Recover, Movable or Land
sections.gist: Returning to the bathhouse from 6b: Rav Huna applies Rav Nachman's rule that consecrating property one can't recover in court is void, and the Gemara reconciles it with R. Yochanan's rule on robbed items by making the bathhouse part of the land.

chart.caption: Consecrating property held by another: when it works
columns: Can the owner recover it in court?
rows: The disputed bathhouse, no proof either way
No
Rav Nachman: property one can't recover in court can't be consecrated
Void
A robbed movable, owner hasn't despaired
Yes
R. Yochanan: not in his possession until he retakes it
Not valid
A bath dug into the ground, owner can prove it
Yes
Land stays in the owner's possession
Valid

children.title: Rav Nachman: No Recovery in Court, No Consecration
children.gist: A case like the bathhouse went up from Rav Chisda to Rav Huna, who ruled by Rav Nachman: property one can't recover in court can't be consecrated.

bullets.text: On 6b the question was whether consecrating a disputed bathhouse works like seizing it, and whether the other side's silence admits ownership.
What was concluded? R. Chiya bar Avin: such a case went from Rav Chisda's school to Rav Huna's school, and Rav Huna resolved it by a statement of Rav Nachman.
Rav Nachman: property one cannot recover from another's possession by legal process is not consecrated if he consecrates it while the other holds it.
Since neither side could prove the bathhouse was his, the consecration was void. So the other party's silence proves nothing: he had no reason to protest an act with no effect.

children.title: R. Yochanan's Robbed Object: A Movable Tub or a Bath in the Ground?
children.gist: If recoverable property can be consecrated, that contradicts R. Yochanan's rule that a robbed item can't be consecrated by its owner; answer: the bathhouse is land, which never leaves its owner's possession.

bullets.text: Inference from Rav Nachman: if he can recover it in court, is his consecration valid even before he takes it back?
But R. Yochanan: a robbed item whose owner hasn't despaired can be consecrated by neither party. The robber can't, because it isn't his; the owner can't, because it isn't in his possession.
Answer: the case is not a movable tub but a bath dug into the ground. Once the owner can recover it in court, it is already in his possession.
Land can't be carried off, so another person's use of it doesn't take it out of the owner's domain (*reshut*). With movables, physical control is what counts.

sections.title: Each Takes What He Holds: Oath, Fringes, Cloth, Get, Gold
sections.gist: Rav Tachalifa's baraita gives each holder the part in his hand; the Gemara squares it with the Mishnah through the fringes, derives from it a rule for acquiring with a cloth (and distinguishes a *get*), and Rava rules on a gold-threaded garment.

children.title: Baraita vs. Mishnah: The Part in Each Hand, or Only the Fringes
children.gist: Each holder takes the part in his hand and the rest is split, with an oath; the Mishnah's plain equal split is where both hold only the fringes.

bullets.text: Rav Tachalifa of the West (Eretz Yisrael) taught before R. Abbahu: two holding a garment each take up to where his hand reaches, and they divide the rest equally.
R. Abbahu signaled with his hand that he should add: "and they take an oath."
Rashi: he pointed heavenward. Even when each keeps what is in his hand, the oath still applies, so that people won't simply grab other people's garments.
Then when does the Mishnah's plain "they divide" apply? Rav Pappa: when neither holds the garment itself, only its fringes (*karkashta*). Each swears and they divide it.

children.title: Rav Mesharshiya: Grasping Three by Three Fingerbreadths of the Cloth
children.gist: From Rav Pappa's statement: *kinyan chalifin* (acquisition by cloth) takes effect once the recipient grasps a 3×3 piece, since that part counts as severed; a *get* on a string is different, because it needs complete severance, not just giving.

bullets.text: Rav Mesharshiya learns from Rav Pappa's statement: in acquisition by cloth (*kinyan chalifin*), the whole cloth need not change hands. Once the recipient grasps three by three fingerbreadths, the minimum size of a cloth that counts as a utensil, the transaction takes effect.
This fulfils the verse on which the cloth acquisition rests: "a man drew off his shoe and gave it to his neighbor" (Ruth 4:7).
Reason: that much is significant enough to count as though cut off from the rest, so grasping it completes the giving even though the rest stays in the other's hand.
The logic comes from the baraita: what is in one's hand is treated as already cut off (*ki'man de'pasik dami*), so it is complete in itself.

children.title: Cloth vs. *Get* on a String: Giving or Complete Severance
children.gist: Rav Chisda's *get* with a string still in the husband's hand seems to contradict Rav Mesharshiya; the Gemara answers that a *get* needs complete severance, which a cloth acquisition doesn't.

bullets.text: Challenge from Rav Chisda: a husband put a *get* in his wife's hand but kept hold of a string tied to it. If he can pull the *get* back to himself, she is not divorced; if he can't, she is divorced.

Answer: a *get* must bring about complete severance (*keritut*) between husband and wife, and there is none while he keeps any hold on it. A cloth acquisition needs only an act of giving, and giving part of the cloth is a real giving.

children.title: Rava's Gold-Threaded Garment: Which Way to Cut?
children.gist: Even gold lying nearer one holder is split equally: he can't insist on a cut that leaves it on his side, because the other can demand a cut the other way.

bullets.text: Rava: even a garment worked with gold thread is divided.
Isn't that obvious? It is needed where the gold lies in the middle, in neither's hand. That too is obvious, since the rest is divided.
It is needed where the gold is nearer one of them, though not in his grasp. He might say "cut it across the middle between us," leaving the gold on his side.
The other replies: "Why cut it that way? Cut it the other way." So the gold is divided equally.
Neither way of cutting is more natural than the other, so neither party can force his choice on the other.

sections.title: Two Holding a Promissory Note: *Kiyum shtar*, a Judge's Custody, Repayment
sections.gist: A baraita on a note held by creditor and debtor, and one that fell to a judge: the Gemara explains Rebbi vs. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel through *kiyum shtar* (ratification), Rava explains the judge clause, and R. Yosi's view is reconciled with a baraita on a found *ketubah*.

children.title: The Baraita: Ratify It, Divide It, Keep It, or Presumptive Status
children.gist: Creditor and debtor both grip a note: Rebbi requires *kiyum shtar*, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel has them divide; a note that fell to a judge is never removed, while R. Yosi says it keeps its presumptive status.

bullets.text: Creditor and debtor both grip a note. Creditor: "It's mine; the debt is unpaid, I dropped it and found it." Debtor: "It was yours, but I repaid you and you gave it to me."
Rebbi: the note must be ratified through its signatories (*kiyum shtar*).
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: they divide.
If the note fell into a judge's hands, it is never removed from him. R. Yosi: it keeps its presumptive status.

children.title: Rebbi vs. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: *Modeh Bi'shtar She'katvo*
children.gist: Rebbi can't mean the ratified note collects in full; Rav Nachman limits the dispute to an unratified note, which only the debtor's admission props up, and the question is whether that admission is enough.

bullets.text: Does Rebbi mean that once ratified, the creditor collects everything? But Rebbi accepts the Mishnah that two holders divide.
Rava citing Rav Nachman: if the note was already ratified, everyone agrees they divide. The dispute is over an unratified note.

Rebbi: even when the debtor admits he wrote the note, the creditor must ratify it (*modeh bi'shtar she'katvo tzarikh le'kaymo*). If he ratifies it, they divide; if he can't, he gets nothing, although the debtor admits the loan.
Reason: an unratified note is a mere shard. Only the debtor's word makes it a note, and that same debtor says it was repaid.
This is *ha'peh she'asar hu ha'peh she'hitir*: the creditor can't use the admission of the debt and ignore the claim of payment that comes with it.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: once the debtor admits writing the note, no *kiyum shtar* is needed. The note stands, and they divide.

Witnesses signed on a note count as though their testimony was already examined in court. *Kiyum shtar* is a rabbinic addition that falls away once the debtor admits the note, so his "I paid" can't undo it.

children.title: 'Fell into a Judge's Hands': A Ratified Note Found by a Stranger
children.gist: Rava reads the clause as a stranger finding a note that bears a court's *kiyum shtar*: even so it isn't returned to the creditor, for fear the debt was repaid.

bullets.text: Why can't a note that fell to a judge be used to collect? Rava: read it as a third party who found a note that had 'fallen to a judge', meaning the court wrote its *kiyum shtar* on it. It is never returned until proof is brought.
Without a *kiyum shtar* it goes without saying, since perhaps the debtor wrote it intending to borrow and never did.
Even when ratified, the finder doesn't return it to the creditor, because we suspect repayment (*chashash pera'on*): the debtor may have paid and then lost the note.

children.title: R. Yosi: Presumptive Status or *Chashash Pera'on*? The Found *Ketubah*
children.gist: R. Yosi ignores possible repayment of a note but suspects it for a widow's or divorcee's *ketubah*; three resolutions: reverse the note baraita and read the *ketubah* baraita as all R. Yosi, Rav Pappa's 'by your own view', and Ravina's two *ketubot*.

chart.caption: Three ways to reconcile R. Yosi on the note with R. Yosi on the found *ketubah*

Rav Pappa

Reversed, as in the first answer
Suspects it, but not during the marriage

children.title: The Contradiction: R. Yosi and the *Ketubah* Found in the Market
children.gist: R. Yosi says a paid debtor would destroy his note, yet he withholds a found *ketubah* from a widow or divorcee lest she was paid.

bullets.text: R. Yosi: the note keeps its presumptive status and we don't suspect repayment, since a debtor who paid would have destroyed the note at once.
Challenge from a baraita: a *ketubah* is found in the market. If the husband admits he hasn't paid, return it to the wife. If he claims he paid, return it to neither.

R. Yosi there: while she is still married, return it to her, since he presumably didn't pay during the marriage. If she is widowed or divorced, return it to neither, since perhaps she was paid. So R. Yosi does suspect repayment.

children.title: Reverse the Note Baraita; the *Ketubah* Baraita Is All R. Yosi
children.gist: Swapping the note baraita's attributions makes the Rabbis contradict themselves, so the *ketubah* baraita is read as a single, abbreviated statement of R. Yosi.

bullets.text: Reverse the note baraita: "never removed" is R. Yosi, and the Rabbis say "it keeps its presumptive status."
Then the Rabbis contradict themselves: here they ignore repayment, but in the *ketubah* baraita they suspect it.
Answer: the *ketubah* baraita is entirely R. Yosi and is abbreviated. "Return it to neither" refers to a widow or divorcee; while she is married it goes back to her, as R. Yosi says.

children.title: Rav Pappa: R. Yosi Argues from the Rabbis' Own View
children.gist: Without reversing, R. Yosi never suspects repayment and was only arguing that the Rabbis should concede the married case; they answer that he may have paid her in bundles of money.

bullets.text: Don't reverse anything. R. Yosi tells the Rabbis: "I don't suspect repayment even after widowhood or divorce. But you, who do, should at least concede that during the marriage it goes back to her, since the *ketubah* isn't yet due."
The Rabbis reply: even during the marriage, perhaps he gave her bundles of money and she handed back the *ketubah*. Returning it would let her collect twice.

children.title: Ravina: The Rabbis Fear Two *Ketubot*, Not Repayment
children.gist: Reversing the note baraita works if the Rabbis' reason in the *ketubah* case is a replacement *ketubah*, not repayment.

bullets.text: Reverse the note baraita after all. The Rabbis' reason in the *ketubah* case is not repayment: once the first was lost, the husband had to write a second, and returning the found one would let her collect twice.
R. Yosi returns it to the wife during the marriage because he doesn't suspect two *ketubot*; he considers that rare.
So the two sides are not only arguing about repayment: in the *ketubah* case each is weighing a different concern.

sections.title: *Tofes* and *Toref*: Does the Part You Hold Change the Split?
sections.gist: R. Elazar gives each holder the part of the note he holds, R. Yochanan says they always divide (the Gemara limits this to a *toref* in the middle), and Ravina explains that holding the *toref* means taking the value its date adds.

children.title: R. Elazar vs. R. Yochanan: *Tofes*, *Toref*, and a *Toref* in the Middle
children.gist: R. Elazar: one takes the *tofes*, the other the *toref*; R. Yochanan's 'always divide' is limited to a *toref* lying between them, which can't be claimed by the nearer side.

bullets.text: R. Elazar: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's "divide" is where both hold the *tofes* (the standard wording) or both hold the *toref* (names, amount and date). If one holds the *tofes* and the other the *toref*, each takes the part he holds.
R. Yochanan: they always divide equally.
Challenge: the garment baraita says each takes up to where his hand reaches. Answer: R. Yochanan means a *toref* lying in the middle, held by neither; where one does hold it, he agrees.
Isn't that obvious? It is needed where the *toref* is nearer one side. He can't demand a cut that leaves it with him, because the other says "cut it the other way, and we'll share it."

returns_to.note: The same 'cut it the other way' reply as in Rava's gold-threaded garment

children.title: What Does the *Toref* Buy? The Value of the Date
children.gist: Half a note is useless paper, so Ravina explains the split as value: the *toref* holder gets what the date adds, the right to collect from *nekhasim meshubadim* (liened property).

bullets.text: Rav Acha of Difti to Ravina: by R. Elazar, what does either one do with his piece? Stop up the mouth of his flask with it?
Ravina: the division is of value, not of paper.

The *toref* holder argues: what is a note with a date worth, and what without? A dated note collects even from liened property the debtor sold after the loan (*nekhasim meshubadim*); an undated one doesn't. The *tofes* holder pays him the difference.
Worked example: a note for 1,000 is worth 950 with a date and 700 without. The *toref* holder takes the 250 difference, the 700 is split 350 each, so he ends with 600 and the other with 350.

Tosafot: why the date? Every other part is needed for the note to be valid at all. Only the date can be missing without invalidating it, costing only the *nekhasim meshubadim*, so it is a separable value.

sections.title: 'They Divide' Means by Value: Garment, Gold Garment, or Animal
sections.gist: Ravina's point holds for every 'they divide' in the chapter: a cut garment might serve for children, even a gold one for royal children, but a non-kosher animal can't be cut up, so division is of value.

bullets.text: Wherever the text says the parties divide, it means the value, not the item itself. Otherwise, would two holding a garment cut it in half and ruin it?
Rejected: they could cut it, since each half is still usable as a garment for small children.
Rava's gold-threaded garment would be ruined by cutting? No: the halves could serve the children of kings or the wealthy.

The Mishnah's two people sitting on an animal: a kosher one could be slaughtered and its meat divided, but a non-kosher one would become worthless. So they must divide its value, and the same holds in every case of dividing.
This is not a technicality: it defines what "they divide" means throughout the chapter, the note included.

key_terms.definition: The Torah's tithe of cattle and sheep: the year's newborn animals pass one by one under a rod, and every tenth is marked as sacred and brought as an offering.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The Gemara asks which 'doubtful' animals may enter the pen to be tithed, since an animal that is already sacred can't become the tithe.

key_terms.sense: redeeming a firstborn donkey with a lamb
key_terms.definition: A firstborn male donkey must be redeemed with a lamb, which is given to a kohen; the lamb itself carries no sanctity.
key_terms.on_this_daf: A lamb that redeemed a doubtful firstborn donkey stays with the Israelite, since the kohen can't prove his claim, and so it can be tithed with his flock.

key_terms.sense: acquisition by handing over a cloth
key_terms.definition: A formal act of acquisition in which one party hands the other an object, usually a cloth, and taking hold of it concludes the transaction, based on the shoe in Ruth 4:7.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Rav Mesharshiya rules that the recipient need only grasp three by three fingerbreadths of the cloth, since giving (unlike a get's severance) can be partial.

key_terms.sense: court ratification of a document's signatures
key_terms.definition: Authenticating the witnesses' signatures on a document before a court, after which the document can be used to collect.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Rebbi requires ratification before a disputed note can be divided; Rava reads 'fell into a judge's hands' as a note bearing the court's ratification.

key_terms.sense: a debtor admitting he wrote the note
key_terms.definition: The case of a debtor who admits that a note against him is genuine but claims he repaid it, and the question whether the creditor must still ratify the note to collect.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Rav Nachman explains Rebbi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel as disputing this: Rebbi requires ratification, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel does not.

key_terms.sense: suspicion that a debt was repaid
key_terms.definition: The concern that a found or disputed document may already have been paid off, so that returning it would allow the creditor to collect twice.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The first tanna suspects repayment of a found ratified note and R. Yosi does not; the Gemara reconciles this with R. Yosi's ruling on a found ketubah.

key_terms.sense: the standard and operative parts of a document
key_terms.definition: The tofes is a document's standard, formulaic wording; the toref is its individual part: the names of the parties, the amount and the date.
key_terms.on_this_daf: R. Elazar gives each holder of a note the part he holds, and Ravina explains this as the toref holder taking the value its date adds.

key_terms.sense: liened property sold to third parties
key_terms.definition: Property the debtor owned when the loan was made and later sold; a creditor holding a dated note can collect from it in the buyer's hands.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The right to collect from liened property is what the date adds, so it measures the value of the toref.

judgment_calls: The section on tithing doubtful animals (7a.2–3) continues the previous daf's sugya about the kohen who seizes the animal; kept as its own top-level section because this daf's scope begins there, with a gist clause tying it back.
The bathhouse section is split into Rav Nachman's principle and the R. Yochanan challenge; it could be one flat section, but the challenge and its answer (movable vs. land) form a distinct step.
Rav Chisda's get on a string is nested under Rav Mesharshiya, since it is a challenge to his derivation; it could be a sibling within the garment section.

The judge clause (Rava, 7a.23–7b.2) is kept separate from the R. Yosi/ketubah discussion, which is split starting at 7b.3, the line where R. Yosi's view is explained; merging them would also be reasonable.

The 'division means value' discussion (7b.19–8a.3) grows out of Ravina's answer on the toref and could be a child of the tofes/toref section; made top-level because it redefines 'they divide' for the whole chapter.

R. Yochanan's toref section carries a returns_to link to Rava's gold garment: the Gemara reuses the same reply rather than literally returning to that discussion, but the link shows the learner the parallel.
coverage_notes: 7a.1 (asiri vadai, the conclusion of the jumping-sheep argument) belongs to the previous daf's outline; the essay's review of whether the holder is ruled the owner is used only as brief shiur framing in s1.
The essay names 'Rav Achai mi-Difti'; the text has Rav Acha of Difti (both at 7a.2 and 7b.16). Followed the text.
The essay has 'Rabba bar Avuha'; the text has Rabba bar Avuh. Followed the text.
The essay has 'Rav Chiya bar Avin'; the Sefaria text has R. Chiya bar Avin. Followed the text.
The essay says Rav Mesharshiya derives his rule from the baraita; the text says he learns it from Rav Pappa's statement. Followed the text, and kept the baraita's logic as shiur framing.
The essay attributes the 'a paid debtor would destroy the note' reasoning to Rashi; the provided text presents it as the Gemara's explanation of R. Yosi. Followed the text.
The essay describes the ketubah baraita's first case as 'the husband admits it fell from the wife'; the text says the husband admits he has not paid. Followed the text.

On Ravina, the essay says R. Yosi is 'implicitly concerned for other reasons' during the marriage; the text says R. Yosi returns the ketubah because he doesn't suspect two ketubot, which he considers rare. Followed the text.

The worked numbers (950/700, 600 vs. 350) and the equal split of the base value are the shiur's illustration; the text says only that the tofes holder pays the toref holder the difference. Marked as shiur.
The essay's section on division as valuation continues into 8a (garments for children, royal children, the animal); all of that falls within this outline's scope (to 8a.3).

charts.subject: The baraita's four rulings (Rebbi, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, the judge clause, R. Yosi)
charts.why_not: The s12 chart covers the main dispute, and the judge clause is explained in its own section; a grid would repeat the bullets.

charts.subject: Cloth acquisition vs. get on a string
charts.why_not: Two cases turning on one distinction (giving vs. severance); the illustration and bullets carry it.

charts.subject: Garment, gold garment and animal: can each be cut?
charts.why_not: A short linear proof ending in one conclusion; a chart adds nothing to the bullets.

illustrations.subject: Creditor and debtor both gripping a note, with their competing claims
illustrations.why_not: The scene is simple and the substance lies in the ratification dispute, which the chart handles better.

illustrations.subject: The found ketubah: returned during the marriage, withheld after widowhood or divorce
illustrations.why_not: Six illustrations already; the three-resolution chart shows the ketubah rulings more usefully.

illustrations.subject: Two people sitting on a non-kosher animal
illustrations.why_not: A vivid image but a one-step proof; lower priority than the tofes/toref value picture.

illustrations.subject: A stranger finding a note with a court's ratification
illustrations.why_not: Hard to show the suspicion of repayment visually beyond a document and a finder.
